newsitem.title: USA: Gag order hearing sheds light on media tactics.
newsitem.headline: Gag order hearing sheds light on media tactics.

text.p: On the eve of a hearing on whether accused infant murderer Amy Grossberg and her lawyer violated a gag order by granting an interview to Barbara Walters, court documents show ABC and Walters courted the lawyer with an offer of "support" and an invitation to a presidential dinner.
The documents cast a rare public light on the high-stakes pursuit by media outlets of hot news stories.

In a letter Feb. 11 to Charles Oberly, Grossberg's former lawyer, Walters wrote, "I do hope we will be able to bring the true story of the Grossberg family to the public. Your dedication to the family is enormously moving. I was affected by them as well and would like to offer any support I can."
Other documents show ABC invited Oberly to a presidential dinner for White House correspondents while the interview negotiations were under way. Oberly did not attend.
A producer for another network programme also offered to help Oberly with referrals to a literary agent to discuss rights to the Grossberg story, the documents show.

ABC representatives and Grossberg's attorneys told Reuters that all discussions held were appropriate and did not compromise the integrity of the interview, which was a Walters exclusive on the ABC newsmagazine "20/20" broadcast June 6.

"Mr. Oberly was personally involved in this case. As I recalled from when they met and were discussing this, he was close to tears ... When Barbara offered support, it was for his need to conform with the gag order if we did an interview," ABC spokesman Martin Blair told Reuters.
"When Barbara meets folks like this, she is very warm and empathic. But (during the interview) she goes right ahead and asks the tough questions," Blair added.

Grossberg and her high school sweetheart, Brian Peterson, face trial Oct. 6 on charges they murdered their newborn son Nov. 12 after delivering him in a Delaware motel room and disposed of his body in a trash bin.
If convicted they could face the death penalty. They are free on $300,000 bail each and are living with their parents.

Prosecutors said in court papers they will ask Superior Court Judge Henry Ridgely Thursday to punish Grossberg and dismiss her current attorney, Robert Gottlieb, for alleged violations of a gag order limiting pre-trial publicity.

Prosecutors have focused on Gottlieb's statement in the 20/20 interview that "Amy should not have been charged. Amy is not guilty." They also have criticised Grossberg for saying in the interview that to call her a "baby killer" was "the furthest thing from the truth."
Gottlieb declined comment except to tell Reuters: "I cannot say enough for the professionalism and integrity of Ms. Walters and her entire staff."
